text: With Coachella going on this weekend, it's a perfect time to talk about hypersexualization of female pop stars. Have you noticed how most performers are now wearing lingerie-inspired outfits on stage? You probably have seen the videos of Sabrina Carpenter and Madonna at Coachella, and that is part of a larger trend. They're all doing it. Taylor Swift, Dua Lipa, Chaperone, Addison Rae, they're all doing it. When you see an entire industry of women doing the same thing, is it really a free individual choice? I'm not sure. I think this is becoming a requirement from the music industry, from the labels, from the producer, from all of these men who are telling women that they need to do that if they want to be noticed, if they want to be taken seriously, and if they're not willing to do it, then there's a thousand other women who are lining up out there who would be willing to do it in their place. So this is the video arguing that female pop stars are basically forced to perform in lingerie-inspired outfits on stage. The lady claims that she thinks that it's not really their choice, that it is becoming a requirement, that it is the men running the labels make them do it, dress like that, or get replaced by the next girl lined up outside the office. Let's see if her statement can withstand any scrutiny, or if it falls apart once you look more closely. First, is the music industry male-dominated? Yes, it seems so. At the top, it's mostly men. Across the biggest companies, women are only about 13.2% of the CEOs and presidents. So if the point is the people signing the checks are mostly men, she is right. No argument from me. But after that, her logic breaks. If men at the top were enforcing a sexy-or-you-are-out rule, it would have to show up everywhere. Same rule for everyone. So let's actually check. Sabrina Carpenter, the lingerie example. She's on Island Records. That's Universal Music Group. Taylor Swift, Republic Records. Also Universal. Billie Eilish, Interscope. Also Universal. Lana Del Rey, Polydor slash Interscope. Again, Universal Music Group. Same parent company, same executives at the top. Now look at what those artists actually do on stage. Sabrina Carpenter is known for the provocative, lingerie-inspired outfits. Taylor Swift will go for bodysuits and shorter, more revealing looks too. But Lana Del Rey's whole image is the opposite direction. Vintage, romantic, usually long-flowing dresses. And Billie Eilish built her entire brand on covering up. Oversized baggy clothes hiding her body on purpose. So that's four of the biggest artists on the planet with four completely different images. From provocative all the way to conservative. Sitting under the same Universal Music Group with the same bosses at the top. And that's the problem for her argument. If the men at the top were really enforcing a dress-sexy-or-you-are-out rule, you couldn't have Billie Eilish covered head-to-toe and Sabrina Carpenter in a lace bodysuit on the same roster. You can't run opposite rules for different women and call it a rule. The look isn't coming down from the executives. It's coming from each artist. Now, she might say, okay, maybe it's not hard rule, but there is still pressure. I'm sure there is pressure. But pressure to do what exactly? Here's the part where theory lives out. A record label is a business. Universal Music Group isn't some guy's private kingdom. It's a publicly traded company. Its job is to make money for shareholders. So labels don't push a look because the men at the top personally like it. They push whatever sells. And that changes the whole story. Because even where the sexy look does show up, it's not men forcing their taste onto women. It's the market rewarding it. And that market is driven heavily by women. In 2024, over 63% of the top pop streams in the US were female artists. And the audience itself seems to skew female. Luminate's data shows artists like Sabrina Carpenter, Charlie XCX, and Chappelle Roan overindexed with women and the LGBTQ plus community. So women aren't being pushed around in pop. They're the ones making it and a big part of who is listening. Look, I'm not saying there is zero pressure in this industry. There is. But that's not what she claimed. She claimed men are pulling the strings and women have no real choice. And when you check the labels, check the rosters, check who is actually winning, that story doesn't hold up. The women who lean into it are choosing it. The women who don't are winning, too. That's not men controlling women. That's women making different calls and the market responding to them.
